explain.say: Have you ever wondered who decided how long a metre is? Look at the first point. In France before 1790 there were hundreds of different measures, and a foot in one town could be longer than in the next. Shopping and trading were a muddle!

explain.say: See the globe at 1791? French scientists wanted a unit that belonged to everyone, taken from Earth itself. They said a metre is one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. Can you imagine measuring a quarter of the planet?

explain.say: That's what they did next. Look at the compass. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent six years measuring from Dunkirk in France to Barcelona in Spain, using triangles and star sightings. Then, at 1799, a platinum bar was made exactly one metre long.

explain.say: Look at 1875. Seventeen countries signed the Metre Convention to share the metric system. Today almost every country uses metres, and every science lab does. What do you measure in metres or centimetres?

explain.say: Well done! See the light at the last point? Since 1983, a metre is the distance light travels in 1 divided by 299,792,458 of a second, so anyone, anywhere, can make a perfect metre. Wow: the old Earth survey was off by only about 0.2 millimetres per metre!

faq.a: Before the 1790s, places used many different units, which made trade and science confusing. French scientists wanted one fair unit, based on nature, for everyone.

faq.q: How was the first metre defined?
faq.a: As one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the line through Paris.

faq.q: How is the metre defined today?
faq.a: Since 1983, the metre has been the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1 divided by 299,792,458 of a second.
asks: What is a metre based on now?

faq.q: Which countries don't use the metric system?
faq.a: The United States still uses miles, feet and pounds for most everyday things, though its scientists use metric. Liberia and Myanmar have used older units too, but both are moving toward metric.

faq.q: How accurate was the first Earth measurement?
faq.a: Very good, but not perfect. The first metre bar came out about 0.2 millimetres shorter than a true ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance.

facts: Since 1983 the metre has been defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
Seventeen countries signed the Metre Convention in Paris in 1875.
